evaluations.name: Correctness parity
evaluations.prompt: Score the correctness of behavior this repository currently implements and claims to support against stable public PyTorch, from 0 to 100. Missing APIs belong exclusively to the separate PyTorch feature coverage evaluation and must not lower this correctness score. Inspect executable Rust, Python, and differential tests and their implementation evidence. Evaluate outputs, shapes, strides, dtypes, devices, errors, aliasing and view semantics, numerical edge cases, autograd behavior, empty tensors, and interactions among supported features. A score of 100 means the supported surface is indistinguishable from PyTorch and comprehensively edge-tested; any regression in previously supported behavior must lower the score.

evaluations.name: PyTorch feature coverage
evaluations.prompt: Score weighted PyTorch feature coverage from 0 to 100 using the fixed area weights and rules in FEATURES.md. Count only stable public Python concepts backed by executable side-by-side semantic tests; Rust-only capabilities, stubs, documentation-only claims, and missing edge-case behavior do not count. Include tensor storage and views, dtypes/devices/dispatch, creation and math, linear algebra, autograd, neural-network APIs, optimizers and data utilities, serialization, compilation and distributed execution, and ecosystem ergonomics. Missing capabilities remain zero in their denominator.

evaluations.name: Performance parity
evaluations.prompt: Score performance parity of behavior this repository currently implements and claims to support against equivalent PyTorch operations, from 0 to 100. Missing APIs belong exclusively to the separate PyTorch feature coverage evaluation and must not lower this performance score; incorrect supported behavior still receives zero performance credit. Apply BENCHMARKING.md: compare equivalent work, release/native execution, symmetric warmup and sampling, representative shapes/layouts/thread counts, geometric aggregation, and protection against dead-code elimination or deferred work. Credit concrete implementation and benchmark evidence rather than isolated favorable microkernels. A score of 100 means the supported workload is broadly at parity with or faster than PyTorch without semantic shortcuts.

evaluations.name: Python API compatibility
evaluations.prompt: Score drop-in compatibility of the torch_rs Python API with stable public PyTorch from 0 to 100. Inspect the exported namespace, function and method signatures, argument forms and defaults, return types, Tensor properties, dtype/device metadata, exception behavior, scalar and sequence handling, views and aliasing, autograd-facing behavior, modules, and ordinary import/package ergonomics. Award credit only for implemented behavior supported by executable compatibility tests, and keep the deliberately unsupported PyTorch surface in the denominator.

evaluations.name: Benchmark integrity
evaluations.prompt: Score the integrity and decision quality of the repository's correctness and performance evidence from 0 to 100. Apply README.md and BENCHMARKING.md: evaluators must be independent from implementation branches, equivalent work must be compared, incorrect and unsupported cells must score zero, seeds and held-out shapes must resist specialization, outputs must be materialized, provenance and environment must be reported, and quick screens must remain strict subsets of final gates. Credit enforced tests and workflows over prose, and penalize editable, asymmetric, gameable, noisy, or irreproducible measurements.

evaluations.name: Sustainable architecture
evaluations.prompt: Score how sustainably the native Rust engine can grow toward broad PyTorch semantics from 0 to 100. Inspect storage/layout/view abstractions, dtype and device dispatch boundaries, operation reuse, autograd graph design, Python bindings, safety, error consistency, modularity, tests, and dependency discipline. Reward clear extensible mechanisms that preserve existing fast paths and semantics. Penalize monolithic dispatch, duplicated per-operation logic, benchmark-specific branches, forwarding production operations to Python or PyTorch, fragile special cases, and architecture that makes the next feature disproportionately risky.
